1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	We organize results around three questions:
5	(1)~which method best detects stagnation across deployment scenarios? (\S\ref{sec:main_results}--\S\ref{sec:robustness});
6	(2)~what drives label quality and cross-coding-agent transfer bottlenecks? (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}--\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation});
7	(3)~can temporal structure in LFs improve labels? (\S\ref{sec:temporal_label_models}).
8	All reported metrics are evaluated against silver labels derived from majority vote over three labeling functions (\S\ref{sec:method}).
9	
10	\paragraph{Circular evaluation caveat.}
11	Structural features (command repetition ratios, file operation counts, edit distances) are computed from the same signals that the labeling functions use to produce silver labels.
12	Consequently, the in-domain structural F1 of 0.995 reflects an upper bound on how well these features can \emph{reverse-engineer} the labeling functions, not detection accuracy against true ground truth.
13	The cross-coding-agent evaluation on OpenHands (0.967 macro-F1) is non-circular: models trained on SWE-Agent LF distributions are tested on a different agent whose LF firing patterns differ substantially (\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}).
14	A human-annotated gold set provides the definitive non-circular evaluation (\S\ref{sec:gold_set}).
15	
16	%-------------------------------------------------------------------
17	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
18	\label{sec:setup}
19	
20	\paragraph{Datasets.}
21	We extract sliding windows of $k{=}5$ consecutive actions from agent trajectories.
22	\textbf{SWE-Agent} trajectories from SWE-bench \citep{jimenez2024swebench,yang2024sweagent} yield 54,809 windows with a stagnation ratio of 28.5\%.
23	\textbf{OpenHands} (OH) trajectories \citep{wang2025openhands} yield 150,652 windows with a stagnation ratio of 20.9\%.
24	Silver labels are produced by majority vote over three labeling functions; confidence equals the number of agreeing LFs (1--3).
25	Train/validation/test splits are constructed at the trajectory level (by SWE-bench instance ID, 70/15/15\%), ensuring no windows from the same task appear across splits.
26	Unless stated otherwise, evaluation uses the conf${\geq}$2 subset: $N{=}1{,}824$ for SWE-Agent (485 stagnation, 1,339 progress) and $N{=}43{,}376$ for OH.
27	
28	\begin{table}[t]
29	\centering
30	\small
31	\begin{tabular}{llrrc}
32	\toprule
33	\textbf{Agent} & \textbf{Source} & \textbf{Windows} & \textbf{Stag\,\%} & \textbf{Conf${\geq}$2} \\
34	\midrule
35	SWE-Agent & SWE-bench & 54,809 & 28.5 & 15,401 \\
36	OpenHands & CodeAct   & 150,652 & 20.9 & 43,376 \\
37	\bottomrule
38	\end{tabular}
39	\caption{Dataset statistics. Stagnation ratios differ substantially across agents, reflecting different action distributions.}
40	\label{tab:dataset_stats}
41	\end{table}
42	
43	\paragraph{Detection methods.}
44	(1)~\textbf{Structural features}: 30 hand-crafted features (repetition rates, file operation counts, edit distances, output entropy) fed to Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), and Gradient Boosting (GB).
45	(2)~\textbf{ProgressProbe}: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B \citep{zhang2025qwen3embedding} embeddings (1024-dim) processed by a 2-layer GRU \citep{cho2014gru} with attention \citep{bahdanau2015attention} (hidden$=$256, dropout$=$0.1), early-stopped at epoch~3 with patience~5.
46	(3)~\textbf{Mean-pool + LR}: Mean-pooled Qwen3 embeddings with logistic regression.
47	(4)~\textbf{LLM-as-Judge}: Claude Sonnet 4.6 zero-shot window-level classification (\$11.66 API cost for the SWE test set).
48	(5)~\textbf{Cosine similarity}: Cosine distance between consecutive window embeddings with a validation-tuned threshold.
49	
50	\paragraph{Metrics.}
51	Macro-F1 is the primary metric. We also report per-class F1 for stagnation (F1\textsubscript{stag}) and progress (F1\textsubscript{prog}).
52	
53	%-------------------------------------------------------------------
54	\subsection{Main Results}
55	\label{sec:main_results}
56	
57	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents in-domain results on the SWE-Agent conf${\geq}$2 test set and cross-coding-agent transfer to OpenHands.
58	
59	\begin{table*}[t]
60	\centering
61	\small
62	\begin{tabular}{l ccc cc}
63	\toprule
64	& \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{SWE-Agent In-Domain} (conf${\geq}$2)} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{OpenHands Transfer}} \\
65	\cmidrule(lr){2-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-6}
66	\textbf{Method} & Macro-F1 & F1\textsubscript{stag} & F1\textsubscript{prog} & All & Conf${\geq}$2 \\
67	\midrule
68	Structural RF$^\dagger$       & \textbf{0.9951} & 0.9928 & 0.9974 & 0.9123 & \textbf{0.9959} \\
69	Structural GB$^\dagger$       & \textbf{0.9951} & 0.9928 & 0.9974 & \textbf{0.9674} & \underline{0.9918} \\
70	Structural LR$^\dagger$       & 0.9874 & 0.9815 & 0.9933 & 0.7801 & 0.9671 \\
71	ProgressProbe (GRU)           & \underline{0.9055} & 0.8593 & 0.9518 & 0.598$^a$ & 0.598$^a$ \\

78	\caption{Stagnation detection results. In-domain evaluation on SWE-Agent conf${\geq}$2 test set ($N{=}1{,}824$) and zero-shot cross-coding-agent transfer to OpenHands. $^\dagger$Structural metrics are evaluated against LF-derived labels and reflect LF-reconstructibility rather than ground-truth accuracy (see circular evaluation caveat). $^a$Probe zero-shot transfer is evaluated on the standard 15\% test split ($N{=}6{,}122$); structural models are evaluated on all OH windows ($N{=}150{,}652$) and the conf${\geq}$2 subset ($N{=}43{,}376$). The structural conf${\geq}$2 numbers provide the most comparable evaluation scope. Probe macro-F1 is identical on all-windows and conf${\geq}$2 subsets (0.598 to three decimal places). For reference, probe zero-shot on the full conf${\geq}$2 set (all 43,376 windows, not just the test split) yields 0.581 macro-F1, consistent with the test-split estimate. $^b$Paired bootstrap on conf${\geq}$2 test split ($N{=}6{,}122$): GB leads fine-tuned probe by 1.65\,pp (95\% CI [1.11, 2.23], $p{<}0.001$); the probe's all-windows advantage (0.976 vs.\ 0.967) reflects stronger performance on conf${=}1$ data. Best in \textbf{bold}, second-best \underline{underlined}.}
79	\label{tab:main_results}
80	\end{table*}
81	
82	In-domain, structural RF achieves 0.995 macro-F1, exceeding the GRU probe by 8.96\,pp (paired bootstrap: 95\% CI [7.44, 10.57]\,pp, $p{<}0.001$).
83	However, the structural--probe gap is inflated by circular evaluation: structural features reconstruct the LFs that generated the labels.
84	The more informative comparison is among non-circular methods: the GRU probe outperforms mean-pool~+~LR by 6.2\,pp, confirming that temporal modeling within windows adds value beyond static embedding aggregation.
85	The zero-shot LLM judge (0.663) underperforms all learned methods despite substantially higher cost (\$11.66 per test set).
86	Extended evaluation with chain-of-thought and few-shot prompting (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_extended}) yields a best LLM macro-F1 of 0.799 (five-shot-CoT, SWE-Agent in-domain), still 16.8\,pp below structural cross-coding-agent transfer (0.967 on OpenHands)---the structural advantage holds even comparing the harder cross-coding-agent setting against the LLM's easier in-domain regime.
87	CoT alone yields gains comparable to few-shot ($+$8.7\,pp vs.\ $+$8.9\,pp over zero-shot); combining them (five-shot-CoT) adds a further $+$4.8\,pp, suggesting complementary mechanisms.
88	Notably, providing the 30 structural features as additional LLM input degrades performance from 0.751 (few-shot) to 0.688, suggesting the signal resides in engineered feature interactions inaccessible to natural language reasoning (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_extended}).
89	
90	%-------------------------------------------------------------------
91	\subsection{Cross-Agent Transfer}
92	\label{sec:cross_agent}
93	
94	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} (right columns) shows models trained on SWE-Agent and evaluated on OpenHands without any OH training data.
95	Structural GB transfers best, achieving 0.967 macro-F1 on all OH windows.
96	RF drops to 0.912 on all-confidence OH data despite matching GB in-domain, suggesting GB's boosted ensemble is more robust to distributional shift.
97	Both structural models exceed 0.99 macro-F1 on conf${\geq}$2 OH windows (GB 0.992, RF 0.996), where label noise is lower.
98	
99	The probe's zero-shot transfer (0.598) lags structural GB by 36.9\,pp---cosine similarity collapses further to 0.447 (mean cosine distance between stagnation and progress windows is 0.610 vs.\ 0.613, showing essentially no class separation)---but full OH fine-tuning closes this gap dramatically: the fine-tuned probe reaches 0.976 macro-F1 on all OH windows, surpassing structural GB (0.967) by 0.9\,pp (\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}).
100	The asymmetry between structural and learned methods is thus stage-dependent: in the zero-data regime, structural features transfer naturally while learned embeddings do not (+36.9\,pp gap); with target-domain fine-tuning, the probe surpasses structural features (+0.9\,pp on all windows).
101	The practical implication is a deployment trade-off: use structural features when no labeled data is available; invest in probe fine-tuning when annotation budget permits.
102	However, this crossover is scope-dependent: on conf${\geq}$2 windows, where label noise is minimal, GB retains its advantage (0.993 vs.\ 0.976; paired bootstrap $p{<}0.001$, $N{=}6{,}122$), suggesting that the probe's all-windows edge reflects better tolerance of noisy low-confidence labels rather than superior high-confidence detection.
103	
104	Paired bootstrap on the matched conf${\geq}$2 test split ($N{=}6{,}122$, 10K resamples) confirms both gaps as significant.
105	The zero-shot probe lags GB by 39.4\,pp on this subset (95\% CI [37.9, 41.0], $p{<}0.001$).
106	The fine-tuned probe narrows the gap but does not close it on conf${\geq}$2: GB retains a 1.65\,pp edge (95\% CI [1.11, 2.23], $p{<}0.001$; GB 0.993, probe 0.976), whereas the probe's advantage on all windows (0.976 vs.\ 0.967) reflects stronger performance on noisier conf${=}1$ labels.
107	
108	\paragraph{Multi-seed stability.}
109	Structural RF: $0.995{\pm}0.000$ in-domain (3 seeds, zero variance); GB cross-coding-agent: $0.968{\pm}0.002$.
110	The probe shows higher variance: $0.919{\pm}0.011$, though all seeds exceed 0.90.
111	
112	%-------------------------------------------------------------------
113	\subsection{Robustness Analysis}
114	\label{sec:robustness}
115	
116	\paragraph{Encoder ablation.}
117	Replacing Qwen3-0.6B with BGE-M3 \citep{chen2024bgem3} or E5-large-v2 \citep{wang2024e5} yields probe macro-F1 of 0.941 and 0.936, respectively (vs.\ 0.906 for Qwen3).
118	All encoders exceed 0.90, indicating the probe's temporal architecture, not a specific encoder, drives performance. Full results appear in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:encoder_ablation}.
119	We use Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (released May 2025) as our primary encoder for recency; BGE-M3 achieves higher F1 (0.941 vs.\ 0.906), confirming encoder-agnostic findings.
120	
121	\paragraph{Architecture ablation.}
122	Replacing the GRU with a Transformer encoder (2-layer, 4-head, same hidden dimension) yields 0.934 macro-F1 vs.\ 0.933 for GRU ($+$0.18\,pp, not significant under paired bootstrap $p{=}0.82$).
123	The two architectures are functionally equivalent on 5-step windows, suggesting that the sequential inductive bias of the GRU provides no advantage at this window length.
124	
125	\paragraph{Window size.}
126	$k{=}5$ is optimal (0.931 macro-F1); $k{=}3$ drops 5.9\,pp and $k{=}7$ drops 1.8\,pp.
127	Shorter windows lack sufficient context; longer windows dilute signal by spanning both progress and stagnation phases.
128	The 0.931 figure differs from the main table's 0.906 because the window ablation uses a separate train/val/test split (seed~42, Qwen3-0.6B encoder) to enable controlled comparison across window sizes; cross-split variance accounts for the gap.
129	Details in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:window_ablation}.
130	
131	\paragraph{Data scaling.}
132	Figure~\ref{fig:data_scaling} compares data efficiency across methods.
133	Structural classifiers are extremely data-efficient: RF achieves 0.991 and GB 0.987 at just 10\% training data, fully saturating by 50\%.
134	The probe scales monotonically from 0.805 (10\%) to 0.906 (100\%) but has not plateaued---a 10.1\,pp drop that is roughly 20$\times$ the structural degradation (${\sim}$0.4--0.8\,pp).
135	This data efficiency further supports the structural signal thesis: the features capture patterns so regular that minimal training data suffices.
136	
137	\begin{figure}[t]
138	\centering
139	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{../../figures/paper/fig_data_scaling.pdf}
140	\caption{Macro-F1 vs.\ training data fraction. Structural classifiers (RF, GB) saturate by 50\% data; the probe scales monotonically but remains 9\,pp below at 100\%.}
141	\label{fig:data_scaling}
142	\end{figure}

145	\subsection{Labeling Function Temporal Dynamics}
146	\label{sec:lf_temporal}
147	
148	We analyze when each LF first fires relative to the onset of stagnation episodes (Table~\ref{tab:lf_temporal}, Figure~\ref{fig:lf_temporal}).

166	The three LFs occupy distinct temporal niches.
167	Command repetition leads stagnation onset by 1.87 steps on average, making it an early warning signal.
168	File diff is near-concurrent ($-1.20$ steps).

173	\paragraph{Cross-agent reversal.}
174	On OpenHands, cmd\_rep shifts from leading ($-1.87$) to lagging ($+3.32$ steps).
175	Under corrected OH labels (\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}), cmd\_rep fires on only 5.4\% of OH windows with 97.9\% precision---a high-precision, low-recall detector whose temporal role differs fundamentally from its SWE-Agent behavior.

185	\subsection{Label Quality and cmd\_rep Coverage}
186	\label{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}
187	
188	A label quality audit revealed that the OH embedding vectors used for silver labeling contained a version mismatch, causing systematic label errors.
189	After correction, the OH stagnation rate on the embedding subset (143,057 windows; short trajectories excluded) shifted from 6.56\% to 21.4\%, with 21,898 window labels flipping.
190	This section quantifies how label quality and cmd\_rep coverage jointly affect probe transfer.
191	
192	\paragraph{Label correction impact on probe transfer.}
193	With corrected labels, the 3-LF probe improves from zero-shot 0.598 to fine-tuned 0.976 (previously 0.7512 under corrupted labels).
194	The improvement is most dramatic at low data fractions: 5\% fine-tuning reaches 0.850, exceeding the old 50\% result (0.69) by 16.0\,pp.
195	The probe converges rapidly: at 50\% OH data it reaches 0.968, essentially matching structural GB (0.967) and demonstrating that the structural advantage is specific to zero-data deployment (full curve in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:cross_agent_cmdrep}).
196	Label quality, not model capacity, was the transfer bottleneck.
197	
198	\paragraph{Prevalence-matched ablation.}
199	To isolate cmd\_rep's contribution, we compare 3-LF and 2-LF (no cmd\_rep) models on the same test set with matched class prevalence.
200	
201	\begin{table}[t]
202	\centering
203	\small
204	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
205	\toprule
206	\textbf{LF Config} & \textbf{Macro-F1} & \textbf{F1\textsubscript{stag}} & \textbf{F1\textsubscript{prog}} \\
207	\midrule
208	3-LF (w/ cmd\_rep) & \textbf{0.9763} & 0.9600 & 0.9930 \\
209	2-LF (no cmd\_rep) & 0.6822 & 0.4810 & 0.8840 \\
210	\midrule
211	$\Delta$ & $-29.4$\,pp & $-47.9$\,pp & $-10.9$\,pp \\
212	\bottomrule
213	\end{tabular}
214	\caption{Prevalence-matched ablation on the same OH test set ($N{=}6{,}122$, stag rate 19.3\%). Removing cmd\_rep drops macro-F1 by 29.4\,pp (McNemar $\chi^2{=}1551$, $p{\approx}0$).}
215	\label{tab:cmd_rep_ablation}
216	\end{table}
217	
218	Removing cmd\_rep drops macro-F1 by 29.4\,pp (McNemar $\chi^2{=}1551$, $p{\approx}0$), a statistically significant degradation driven primarily by stagnation recall ($-47.9$\,pp F1\textsubscript{stag}).
219	
220	\paragraph{Coverage, not label quality, explains the gap.}
221	The 29.4\,pp drop is not caused by cmd\_rep improving label accuracy.
222	After correction, cmd\_rep fires on only 5.39\% of OH windows (down from the previously reported 92.2\% under corrupted embeddings) with 97.91\% precision---a high-precision, low-recall signal.
223	On the 4,070 windows where both 2-LF and 3-LF labels are defined, the two configurations agree on 100\% of labels: cmd\_rep does not change any label where the other two LFs already vote.
224	Its contribution is purely \emph{coverage}: including cmd\_rep expands the training set from ${\sim}$4K to ${\sim}$43K windows (a ${\sim}$10$\times$ increase).
225	The 2-LF model's low F1 reflects data volume collapse---too few training examples to learn the stagnation distribution---rather than label corruption.
226	
227	\paragraph{Implications for weak supervision.}
228	These results reframe how labeling functions contribute to weak supervision pipelines.
229	A high-precision, low-recall LF like cmd\_rep may appear redundant when its labels are a subset of the majority vote, yet removing it causes training data to collapse by an order of magnitude.
230	In prevalence-matched evaluation, this data reduction manifests as a 29.4\,pp F1 drop.
231	The core contribution of such LFs is coverage provision, not label refinement: they extend the labelable portion of the input space rather than correcting other LFs' errors.
232

234	\subsection{Temporal Label Models}
235	\label{sec:temporal_label_models}
236	
237	We investigate whether any label aggregation method---temporal or generative---improves over majority vote (MV).
238	Table~\ref{tab:temporal_models} compares five label models: three temporal (TWV, Lag-HMM, HMM) \citep{ratner2017snorkel,safranchik2020linkedhmm} and two generative i.i.d.\ models (FlyingSquid \citep{fu2020flyingsquid}, Snorkel MeTaL \citep{ratner2019snorkelmetal}).

Conf${\geq}$2 F1: each model's labels evaluated against MV labels on conf${\geq}$2 windows. $^\ast$MV conf${\geq}$2 F1 (0.8946) reflects downstream probe performance when trained on MV labels, not self-agreement (which would be 1.0). $^\ddagger$Downstream probe trained on each method's full labels, evaluated on the SWE-Agent test set ($N{=}8{,}101$) against MV labels. ``---'' = not evaluated downstream. No model consistently improves over MV.}
260	\label{tab:temporal_models}
261	\end{table}
262	
263	\paragraph{Temporal models.}
264	TWV achieves the highest conf${\geq}$2 F1 (0.900, $+$0.6\,pp over MV), but this gain does not propagate downstream: a probe trained on TWV labels scores 0.821 vs.\ 0.847 for MV-trained ($-$2.57\,pp).
265	TWV flips 14.1\% of conf${=}$1 labels, introducing noise that hurts probe training.
266	The Gaussian kernel bandwidth $\sigma$ is critical: $\sigma{=}2$ is optimal; $\sigma{=}1$ drops to 0.811 and $\sigma{=}5$ to 0.808, making TWV impractical as a drop-in MV replacement.
267	HMM overpredicts stagnation (29,176 vs.\ 25,633 progress windows), degrading conf${\geq}$2 F1 by 14.4\,pp and downstream performance to 0.656.
268	Lag-HMM closely tracks MV ($-$0.1\,pp) despite explicitly modeling temporal offsets.
269	
270	\paragraph{Generative (i.i.d.) models.}
271	FlyingSquid \citep{fu2020flyingsquid}, a closed-form triplet-based model, drops 11.3\,pp below MV.
272	On the full dataset, agreement with MV is 82\%; all divergent labels flip progress$\to$stagnation, introducing systematic stagnation bias.
273	Snorkel MeTaL \citep{ratner2019snorkelmetal} fails catastrophically ($-$63.6\,pp), with only 42.3\% MV agreement.
274	Both models assume conditional independence among LFs---an assumption violated by the shared behavioral signals underlying our three LFs---and lack the sequential structure to recover from this misspecification.
275	
276	\paragraph{Root cause: insufficient inter-LF conflict.}
277	These results constitute a negative finding: five label models spanning temporal aggregation and generative modeling all fail to improve over majority vote.
278	Three binary LFs produce at most $2^3{=}8$ voting patterns; conf${\geq}$2 windows dominate the training set, leaving insufficient ambiguity for any aggregation method to exploit.
279	The bottleneck is LF quantity, not aggregation sophistication---scaling to ${>}$10 LFs with higher disagreement rates is needed before advanced label models can add value.
280	In the current 3-LF, low-conflict regime (conf${\geq}$2 agreement rate 95.1\%), temporal alignment gains are offset by noise introduction.
281	With 5--10 LFs generating higher disagreement rates, temporal models may add value---this remains an open question.
282	
283	%-------------------------------------------------------------------
284	\subsection{Gold Set Validation}
285	\label{sec:gold_set}
286	We construct a stratified gold set of 650 windows for non-circular evaluation.
287	Windows are sampled along two axes: \emph{confidence} (balanced across conf${=}1$, conf${=}2$, and conf${=}3$ strata to capture the full ambiguity spectrum) and \emph{trajectory position} (early, middle, and late thirds, since stagnation dynamics differ across trajectory phases; \S\ref{sec:error_analysis}).
288	
289	\paragraph{Annotation protocol.}
290	Two annotators independently label each window as stagnation or progress using an operational definition: \emph{a window is stagnation if the agent's actions within it do not make meaningful progress toward solving the task, regardless of whether the actions appear diverse or purposeful}.
291	Annotators receive the $k{=}5$ action descriptions with full command outputs and file diffs, but \emph{not} the task outcome (resolved/unresolved), preventing information leakage from $\lambda_3$.
292	Disagreements are resolved by a third annotator.
293	Gold validation results are pending; in the interim, cross-coding-agent transfer (\S\ref{sec:cross_agent}) and the feature overlap ablation (\S\ref{sec:feature_overlap}) provide non-circular evidence that structural features encode genuine stagnation signals rather than LF artifacts.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We organize results around three questions:
(1)~which method best detects stagnation across deployment scenarios? (\S\ref{sec:main_results}--\S\ref{sec:robustness});
(2)~what drives label quality and cross-coding-agent transfer bottlenecks? (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}--\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation});
(3)~can temporal structure in LFs improve labels? (\S\ref{sec:temporal_label_models}).
All reported metrics are evaluated against silver labels derived from majority vote over three labeling functions (\S\ref{sec:method}).

\paragraph{Circular evaluation caveat.}
Structural features (command repetition ratios, file operation counts, edit distances) are computed from the same signals that the labeling functions use to produce silver labels.
Consequently, the in-domain structural F1 of 0.995 reflects an upper bound on how well these features can \emph{reverse-engineer} the labeling functions, not detection accuracy against true ground truth.
The cross-coding-agent evaluation on OpenHands (0.967 macro-F1) is non-circular: models trained on SWE-Agent LF distributions are tested on a different agent whose LF firing patterns differ substantially (\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}).
A human-annotated gold set provides the definitive non-circular evaluation (\S\ref{sec:gold_set}).

Unless stated otherwise, evaluation uses the conf${\geq}$2 subset: $N{=}1{,}824$ for SWE-Agent (485 stagnation, 1,339 progress) and $N{=}43{,}376$ for OH.

\subsection{Cross-Agent Transfer}
\label{sec:cross_agent}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} (right columns) shows models trained on SWE-Agent and evaluated on OpenHands without any OH training data.
Structural GB transfers best, achieving 0.967 macro-F1 on all OH windows.
RF drops to 0.912 on all-confidence OH data despite matching GB in-domain, suggesting GB's boosted ensemble is more robust to distributional shift.
Both structural models exceed 0.99 macro-F1 on conf${\geq}$2 OH windows (GB 0.992, RF 0.996), where label noise is lower.

The probe's zero-shot transfer (0.598) lags structural GB by 36.9\,pp---cosine similarity collapses further to 0.447 (mean cosine distance between stagnation and progress windows is 0.610 vs.\ 0.613, showing essentially no class separation)---but full OH fine-tuning closes this gap dramatically: the fine-tuned probe reaches 0.976 macro-F1 on all OH windows, surpassing structural GB (0.967) by 0.9\,pp (\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}).
The asymmetry between structural and learned methods is thus stage-dependent: in the zero-data regime, structural features transfer naturally while learned embeddings do not (+36.9\,pp gap); with target-domain fine-tuning, the probe surpasses structural features (+0.9\,pp on all windows).
The practical implication is a deployment trade-off: use structural features when no labeled data is available; invest in probe fine-tuning when annotation budget permits.
However, this crossover is scope-dependent: on conf${\geq}$2 windows, where label noise is minimal, GB retains its advantage (0.993 vs.\ 0.976; paired bootstrap $p{<}0.001$, $N{=}6{,}122$), suggesting that the probe's all-windows edge reflects better tolerance of noisy low-confidence labels rather than superior high-confidence detection.

Paired bootstrap on the matched conf${\geq}$2 test split ($N{=}6{,}122$, 10K resamples) confirms both gaps as significant.
The zero-shot probe lags GB by 39.4\,pp on this subset (95\% CI [37.9, 41.0], $p{<}0.001$).
The fine-tuned probe narrows the gap but does not close it on conf${\geq}$2: GB retains a 1.65\,pp edge (95\% CI [1.11, 2.23], $p{<}0.001$; GB 0.993, probe 0.976), whereas the probe's advantage on all windows (0.976 vs.\ 0.967) reflects stronger performance on noisier conf${=}1$ labels.

\paragraph{Multi-seed stability.}
Structural RF: $0.995{\pm}0.000$ in-domain (3 seeds, zero variance); GB cross-coding-agent: $0.968{\pm}0.002$.
The probe shows higher variance: $0.919{\pm}0.011$, though all seeds exceed 0.90.

\subsection{Robustness Analysis}
\label{sec:robustness}

\paragraph{Encoder ablation.}
Replacing Qwen3-0.6B with BGE-M3 \citep{chen2024bgem3} or E5-large-v2 \citep{wang2024e5} yields probe macro-F1 of 0.941 and 0.936, respectively (vs.\ 0.906 for Qwen3).
All encoders exceed 0.90, indicating the probe's temporal architecture, not a specific encoder, drives performance. Full results appear in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:encoder_ablation}.
We use Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (released May 2025) as our primary encoder for recency; BGE-M3 achieves higher F1 (0.941 vs.\ 0.906), confirming encoder-agnostic findings.

\paragraph{Architecture ablation.}
Replacing the GRU with a Transformer encoder (2-layer, 4-head, same hidden dimension) yields 0.934 macro-F1 vs.\ 0.933 for GRU ($+$0.18\,pp, not significant under paired bootstrap $p{=}0.82$).
The two architectures are functionally equivalent on 5-step windows, suggesting that the sequential inductive bias of the GRU provides no advantage at this window length.

\paragraph{Window size.}
$k{=}5$ is optimal (0.931 macro-F1); $k{=}3$ drops 5.9\,pp and $k{=}7$ drops 1.8\,pp.
Shorter windows lack sufficient context; longer windows dilute signal by spanning both progress and stagnation phases.
The 0.931 figure differs from the main table's 0.906 because the window ablation uses a separate train/val/test split (seed~42, Qwen3-0.6B encoder) to enable controlled comparison across window sizes; cross-split variance accounts for the gap.
Details in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:window_ablation}.

Figure~\ref{fig:data_scaling} compares data efficiency across methods.

\subsection{Label Quality and cmd\_rep Coverage}
\label{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}

A label quality audit revealed that the OH embedding vectors used for silver labeling contained a version mismatch, causing systematic label errors.
After correction, the OH stagnation rate on the embedding subset (143,057 windows; short trajectories excluded) shifted from 6.56\% to 21.4\%, with 21,898 window labels flipping.
This section quantifies how label quality and cmd\_rep coverage jointly affect probe transfer.

\paragraph{Label correction impact on probe transfer.}
With corrected labels, the 3-LF probe improves from zero-shot 0.598 to fine-tuned 0.976 (previously 0.7512 under corrupted labels).
The improvement is most dramatic at low data fractions: 5\% fine-tuning reaches 0.850, exceeding the old 50\% result (0.69) by 16.0\,pp.
The probe converges rapidly: at 50\% OH data it reaches 0.968, essentially matching structural GB (0.967) and demonstrating that the structural advantage is specific to zero-data deployment (full curve in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:cross_agent_cmdrep}).
Label quality, not model capacity, was the transfer bottleneck.

\paragraph{Prevalence-matched ablation.}
To isolate cmd\_rep's contribution, we compare 3-LF and 2-LF (no cmd\_rep) models on the same test set with matched class prevalence.

Removing cmd\_rep drops macro-F1 by 29.4\,pp (McNemar $\chi^2{=}1551$, $p{\approx}0$), a statistically significant degradation driven primarily by stagnation recall ($-47.9$\,pp F1\textsubscript{stag}).

\paragraph{Coverage, not label quality, explains the gap.}
The 29.4\,pp drop is not caused by cmd\_rep improving label accuracy.
After correction, cmd\_rep fires on only 5.39\% of OH windows (down from the previously reported 92.2\% under corrupted embeddings) with 97.91\% precision---a high-precision, low-recall signal.
On the 4,070 windows where both 2-LF and 3-LF labels are defined, the two configurations agree on 100\% of labels: cmd\_rep does not change any label where the other two LFs already vote.
Its contribution is purely \emph{coverage}: including cmd\_rep expands the training set from ${\sim}$4K to ${\sim}$43K windows (a ${\sim}$10$\times$ increase).
The 2-LF model's low F1 reflects data volume collapse---too few training examples to learn the stagnation distribution---rather than label corruption.

\paragraph{Implications for weak supervision.}
These results reframe how labeling functions contribute to weak supervision pipelines.
A high-precision, low-recall LF like cmd\_rep may appear redundant when its labels are a subset of the majority vote, yet removing it causes training data to collapse by an order of magnitude.
In prevalence-matched evaluation, this data reduction manifests as a 29.4\,pp F1 drop.
The core contribution of such LFs is coverage provision, not label refinement: they extend the labelable portion of the input space rather than correcting other LFs' errors.

\paragraph{Temporal models.}
TWV achieves the highest conf${\geq}$2 F1 (0.900, $+$0.6\,pp over MV), but this gain does not propagate downstream: a probe trained on TWV labels scores 0.821 vs.\ 0.847 for MV-trained ($-$2.57\,pp).
TWV flips 14.1\% of conf${=}$1 labels, introducing noise that hurts probe training.
The Gaussian kernel bandwidth $\sigma$ is critical: $\sigma{=}2$ is optimal; $\sigma{=}1$ drops to 0.811 and $\sigma{=}5$ to 0.808, making TWV impractical as a drop-in MV replacement.
HMM overpredicts stagnation (29,176 vs.\ 25,633 progress windows), degrading conf${\geq}$2 F1 by 14.4\,pp and downstream performance to 0.656.
Lag-HMM closely tracks MV ($-$0.1\,pp) despite explicitly modeling temporal offsets.

\paragraph{Generative (i.i.d.) models.}
FlyingSquid \citep{fu2020flyingsquid}, a closed-form triplet-based model, drops 11.3\,pp below MV.
On the full dataset, agreement with MV is 82\%; all divergent labels flip progress$\to$stagnation, introducing systematic stagnation bias.
Snorkel MeTaL \citep{ratner2019snorkelmetal} fails catastrophically ($-$63.6\,pp), with only 42.3\% MV agreement.
Both models assume conditional independence among LFs---an assumption violated by the shared behavioral signals underlying our three LFs---and lack the sequential structure to recover from this misspecification.

\paragraph{Root cause: insufficient inter-LF conflict.}
These results constitute a negative finding: five label models spanning temporal aggregation and generative modeling all fail to improve over majority vote.
Three binary LFs produce at most $2^3{=}8$ voting patterns; conf${\geq}$2 windows dominate the training set, leaving insufficient ambiguity for any aggregation method to exploit.
The bottleneck is LF quantity, not aggregation sophistication---scaling to ${>}$10 LFs with higher disagreement rates is needed before advanced label models can add value.
In the current 3-LF, low-conflict regime (conf${\geq}$2 agreement rate 95.1\%), temporal alignment gains are offset by noise introduction.
With 5--10 LFs generating higher disagreement rates, temporal models may add value---this remains an open question.

\subsection{Gold Set Validation}
\label{sec:gold_set}
We construct a stratified gold set of 650 windows for non-circular evaluation.
Windows are sampled along two axes: \emph{confidence} (balanced across conf${=}1$, conf${=}2$, and conf${=}3$ strata to capture the full ambiguity spectrum) and \emph{trajectory position} (early, middle, and late thirds, since stagnation dynamics differ across trajectory phases; \S\ref{sec:error_analysis}).

\paragraph{Annotation protocol.}
Two annotators independently label each window as stagnation or progress using an operational definition: \emph{a window is stagnation if the agent's actions within it do not make meaningful progress toward solving the task, regardless of whether the actions appear diverse or purposeful}.
Annotators receive the $k{=}5$ action descriptions with full command outputs and file diffs, but \emph{not} the task outcome (resolved/unresolved), preventing information leakage from $\lambda_3$.
Disagreements are resolved by a third annotator.
Gold validation results are pending; in the interim, cross-coding-agent transfer (\S\ref{sec:cross_agent}) and the feature overlap ablation (\S\ref{sec:feature_overlap}) provide non-circular evidence that structural features encode genuine stagnation signals rather than LF artifacts.

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Circular Evaluation and Its Implications}
\label{sec:circular}

The structural RF's 0.995 macro-F1 (\S\ref{sec:main_results}) is a predictable consequence of feature--label overlap, not a detection achievement.
The 30 structural features include repetition ratios and file operation counts---the same signals $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ consume to produce silver labels.
This score therefore represents an upper bound on LF reverse-engineering fidelity (a feature overlap ablation in \S\ref{sec:feature_overlap} quantifies this decomposition).

Three evaluation settings break this circularity.
First, cross-coding-agent transfer: GB trained on SWE-Agent LF distributions achieves 0.967 macro-F1 on OpenHands, where LF firing patterns differ substantially (e.g., cmd\_rep votes stagnation on 5.4\% vs.\ 65.5\% of windows).
The model cannot memorize LF outputs when tested on a different agent's distribution.
Second, instance isolation: removing 284 SWE-bench task instances (8.3\% of OH test data) that appear in both training and test sets changes all cross-coding-agent macro-F1 by ${<}$0.1\,pp (Table~\ref{tab:instance_isolation}), ruling out instance memorization as an explanation for transfer performance.
Third, a human-annotated gold set (\S\ref{sec:gold_set}) will provide definitive non-circular ground truth.
Until then, all in-domain structural metrics should be interpreted as LF-agreement scores rather than detection accuracy.

\subsection{Feature Overlap Ablation}
\label{sec:feature_overlap}

To quantify how much of the structural classifier's performance derives from LF-overlapping features versus residual signal, we partition the 30 features into two groups.
A feature is classified as \emph{LF-overlapping} if it directly computes the same function as any labeling function: command uniqueness and repetition ratios, adjacent command similarity scores ($\lambda_1$), edit and search command counts and ratios, file display counts ($\lambda_2$), and the short-trajectory indicator ($\lambda_3$).
This yields 11 LF-overlapping and 19 residual features (full classification in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:feature_defs}).
Table~\ref{tab:feature_overlap} reports GB performance for each subset.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature Set} & \textbf{\#Feat} & \textbf{In-Dom.} & \textbf{Cross-Ag.} \\
\midrule
Full (all 30) & 30 & 0.9951 & 0.9674 \\
LF-overlap only & 11 & 0.9937 & \textbf{0.9770} \\
Residual only & 19 & 0.9515 & 0.5656 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\emph{Leave-one-group-out (cross-coding-agent)}} \\
$-$ cmd\_rep ($\lambda_1$) & 25 & --- & 0.5620 \\
$-$ file\_diff ($\lambda_2$) & 25 & --- & 0.6590 \\
$-$ outcome\_bp ($\lambda_3$) & 29 & --- & 0.9660 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Feature overlap ablation (GB). In-Dom.\ = SWE-Agent in-domain macro-F1; Cross-Ag.\ = SWE-Agent $\to$ OpenHands zero-shot. Top: on all OH windows, LF-overlap features alone exceed the full model cross-coding-agent ($+$1.0\,pp; on conf${\geq}$2, direction reverses by $-$0.71\,pp); residual features collapse. Bottom: removing each LF-group individually; cmd\_rep features account for the largest transfer drop ($-$40.6\,pp).}
\label{tab:feature_overlap}
\end{table}

Three findings emerge.
First, on all OH windows ($N{=}150{,}652$), 11 LF-overlapping features alone achieve 0.977 cross-coding-agent F1---exceeding the full 30-feature model (0.967) by 1.0\,pp.
This is the opposite of what label leakage would predict: if these features merely reconstructed the labeling pipeline, adding more features could only help or be neutral, not hurt.
The improvement under fewer features reflects a regularization effect: the 19 residual features encode agent-specific patterns that introduce noise harmful to cross-coding-agent generalization.
(On the conf${\geq}$2 subset, the direction reverses: the full model leads by 0.71\,pp, indicating that residual features contribute positively when label noise is low; the all-windows advantage of LF-overlap features reflects their robustness to noisy conf${=}1$ labels.)

Second, residual features retain non-trivial in-domain signal: 19 features achieve 0.952 macro-F1, confirming that stagnation manifests in patterns beyond what the three LFs capture---text length statistics, trajectory counts, and output statistics carry independent diagnostic value.
However, this signal is agent-specific: cross-coding-agent F1 collapses to 0.566, near the majority baseline (${\sim}$0.55).

Third, LF alignment is evidence of correct LF design, not circularity.
The features that generalize across coding agents are precisely those encoding universal stagnation signals---command repetition patterns and file operation dynamics---rather than agent-specific idiosyncrasies captured by residual features.
One might object that LF-overlapping features merely reconstruct the label-generation pipeline rather than detecting real stagnation.
Two observations counter this.
First, the cross-coding-agent evaluation is itself non-circular: the SWE-Agent LF firing distribution differs drastically from OpenHands (e.g., cmd\_rep fires on 65.5\% vs.\ 5.4\% of windows), so a model that merely memorizes LF outputs would fail on the target agent---yet structural GB achieves 0.967.
Second, if cross-coding-agent success were an artifact of label reconstruction, removing LF-overlapping features should \emph{not} degrade cross-coding-agent performance (the residual features would reconstruct equally well); instead it collapses to 0.566, confirming that the LF-overlapping features encode genuinely transferable stagnation signals rather than pipeline-specific artifacts.

A leave-one-group-out ablation (Table~\ref{tab:feature_overlap}, bottom) further localizes the transfer signal.
Removing the five cmd\_rep features ($\lambda_1$: repetition ratios and adjacent command similarity) drops cross-coding-agent F1 by 40.6\,pp to 0.562; removing the five file\_diff features ($\lambda_2$: edit/search counts and file display) drops it by 30.8\,pp to 0.659.
In contrast, removing the single outcome\_bp feature ($\lambda_3$: is\_short\_trajectory) costs only 0.2\,pp (0.966).
Command repetition patterns are thus the dominant carrier of cross-coding-agent transfer, consistent with their role as a universal stagnation signal (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}).

\subsection{Why No Label Model Improves Over Majority Vote}
\label{sec:why_tlm_fail}

Despite clear temporal structure in LF activations (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}), no label model---temporal or generative---improves downstream detection over majority vote (\S\ref{sec:temporal_label_models}).
The failure spans five models with distinct inductive biases: TWV and Lag-HMM model temporal dynamics, HMM captures latent state transitions, while FlyingSquid and Snorkel MeTaL assume conditional independence.
All fail for the same root cause: three binary LFs produce at most $2^3{=}8$ voting patterns, and conf${\geq}$2 windows dominate the training set, leaving insufficient inter-LF conflict for any aggregation method to exploit.

The failure modes differ by model class.
Temporal models either introduce noise (TWV: $-$2.57\,pp downstream despite $+$0.6\,pp self-evaluated) or overpredict stagnation (HMM: $-$14.4\,pp).
Generative models fare worse: FlyingSquid ($-$11.3\,pp) introduces systematic stagnation bias, and Snorkel MeTaL collapses catastrophically ($-$63.6\,pp, 42.3\% MV agreement).
Both assume conditional independence among LFs---violated by the shared behavioral signals underlying our three functions---and lack sequential structure to recover from this misspecification.

The bottleneck is LF quantity, not aggregation sophistication.
Three binary LFs represent a realistic operating point for domain-specific agent monitoring, where each LF requires expert knowledge of agent failure modes.
Our finding that temporal label models fail in this low-LF regime has direct implications for practitioners who cannot afford to design ${>}$10 labeling functions: majority vote is not merely a convenient baseline but the recommended aggregation strategy.
Scaling to a richer LF set with higher disagreement rates would be needed to create the ambiguity where advanced aggregation could add value \citep{ratner2017snorkel}.

\subsection{Error Analysis}
\label{sec:error_analysis}

We analyze errors of the ProgressProbe (GRU) on the SWE-Agent conf${\geq}$2 test set under the stagnation-positive convention (positive = stagnation throughout).
The model misclassifies 131 of 1,824 windows (7.2\% error rate): 85 false negatives (predicted progress, actual stagnation; 64.9\% of errors) and 46 false positives (predicted stagnation, actual progress; 35.1\%).

The recall bottleneck is the dominant failure mode: $P_\text{stag}{=}0.897$ vs.\ $R_\text{stag}{=}0.825$.
Missed stagnation windows (FN) are not borderline cases---the model assigns them a mean stagnation probability of only 0.078 (i.e., high progress confidence of 0.922), with 73\% receiving $>$0.9 progress probability.
These windows feature agents performing diverse edits and varied commands that mimic progress patterns while making no effective headway, constituting a systematic blind spot.
False positives arise when agents repeat specific command patterns during genuine progress.

LF conflict is a strong error predictor: 39.7\% of error windows have at least one LF disagreeing, compared to a 31\% base rate.
The cmd\_rep LF contributes the highest per-LF error rate (12.75\%).
Errors concentrate in trajectory midpoints (10.2\% error rate vs.\ 6.5\% at endpoints), where the boundary between exploration and stagnation is most ambiguous.
Error mass is also non-uniform across trajectories: the two highest-error trajectories account for 18.3\% of all misclassifications.

\subsection{Cross-Agent Error Patterns}
\label{sec:cross_agent_errors}

We extend error analysis to cross-coding-agent transfer, evaluating the SWE-trained probe and structural GB on the full OH conf${\geq}$2 set (43,376 windows).
The probe misclassifies 19.9\% of windows, while structural GB errs on only 0.51\% (223 windows)---a nearly 40$\times$ gap that quantifies the distributional shift penalty for learned embeddings.
Of the probe's errors, 80.5\% are false positives (predicting stagnation on progress windows), indicating that the probe systematically misreads OH action patterns as stagnation signals learned from SWE-Agent.

The two models' errors are nearly disjoint: only 2.2\% of probe errors overlap with structural errors (192 of 8,643 probe-error windows).
Structural features, being agent-agnostic by construction, are immune to the embedding distribution shift that drives probe failures.

The probe's cross-coding-agent errors are not borderline: 62\% occur at high confidence ($>$0.9 or $<$0.1), ruling out threshold tuning as a remedy.
The embedding space encodes SWE-Agent--specific stagnation patterns that confidently misfire on OH distributions, explaining why even 5\% target fine-tuning (reaching 0.850 macro-F1) dramatically outperforms zero-shot transfer.

\subsection{Outcome Backpropagation as Distant Supervision}
\label{sec:ob_analysis}

Outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) is a privileged signal that uses task outcome, unavailable at inference time.
A 3-seed split-isolated holdout removing $\lambda_3$ yields macro-F1 of $0.770{\pm}0.022$, a 7.7\,pp drop from the 3-LF baseline of 0.847.
$\lambda_3$ contributes 33.5\% of conf${\geq}$2 labels (5,158 of 15,401 windows).

However, $\lambda_3$ functions as a coverage expander rather than an independent corrector: across 43,402 windows where both 2-LF and 3-LF configurations produce labels, their agreement is 100\%.
$\lambda_3$ never flips a majority vote---it only promotes conf${=}1$ windows to conf${=}2$ by adding a third agreeing vote.
This suggests that additional real-time LFs targeting the same coverage gaps could replace the privileged outcome signal without sacrificing label quality.
